newsitem.title: USA: American insurers look to active year.
newsitem.headline: American insurers look to active year.

text.p: U.S. personal property insurers are expected to accelerate mergers and acquisitions in 1997, and life and health insurance sectors are likely to remain hotbeds of deal-making activity, industry sources say.

The insurance industry overall is likely to keep Wall Street nearly as busy this year as it was in 1996, when a record 281 deals valued at $23.1 billion were announced. That compares with 247 deals valued at $24.9 billion in 1995, according to Securities Data Co.

Some of 1996's biggest property-casualty deals included the sale of Aetna's property-casualty business to Travelers Group Inc. for $4 billion and the purchase of American Re Corp. by Germany's Munich Re for $3.3 billion.
In the life insurance sector, the Dutch Aegon NV group agreed to buy the life insurance business of Providian Corp. in a deal worth about $3.5 billion.
General Electric Co.'s GE Capital Corp. bought First Colony Corp. for $1.8 billion and Provident Cos. Inc. agreed to buy Paul Revere Corp. for $1.2 billion.
In the insurance brokerage sector, Aon Corp. agreed to buy Alexander & Alexander Services Inc. for about $1.23 billion.
More potentially large deals are in the pipeline, some Wall Street bankers said, as more foreign buyers seek to expand their presence in the important U.S. market.
"There are certainly significant transactions in the financial institutions sector percolating," said James MacNaughton, head of the financial institutions group at Salomon Brothers.
Deals expected in 1997 include the sale of Chubb Corp.'s life insurance business and the sale of at least some of Xerox Corp.'s property-casualty insurance businesses.

Wall Street buyout firm Kohlberg Kravis & Roberts had agreed to buy Xerox's Talegen insurance businesses in January 1996 for about $2.7 billion, but the deal fell apart in September, leaving Xerox in search of new buyers for the five units.
Meanwhile, CIGNA Corp. and Prudential Insurance Co. of America are expected to give serious thought to the future of their health insurance businesses.
"You can assume they are actively considering whether they want to get bigger or smaller," one investment banker said. "That would also include companies that have already made big acquisitions."
Aetna, after selling its property-casualty business this year, bought U.S. Healthcare Inc. for $8.9 billion.
And The Hartford, which has a new chief executive this year, may consider reshaping its multi-line businesses as well.
But it is the property-casualty sector, especially the personal lines business, that is likely to see the biggest increase in the level of merger activity.

"I think you're going to see a continuation of the activity in the life area and then I think you're going to see, frankly, more activity in the primary property-casualty area," said Robert Goodman, managing director in charge of the insurance group at Wasserstein Perella.
So far, most of the property-casualty deals have arisen from special, distressed situations or they came from the reinsurance industry, which is further along in its consolidation.
